title: How High Is Inflation, Really?
question: How high is US inflation right now, compared with the target, the past and the 2022 peak?
alternates: Is There Really No Inflation? The September 2026 Numbers
Inflation in 2026: High, Low, or Neither?
premise: Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September 2026 and 3.7% over twelve months, so the claim that there is no inflation is wrong. 3.7% is below the 9.1% peak of June 2022 but above every reading in 2024 and 2025, above the roughly 1.5-2.5% pace before the pandemic, and above the 3.0% of January 2025. It was a different story in January 2026: 2.4%, tied for the lowest reading since early 2021 and about the pre-pandemic pace, so 'low by historical standards' was fair then (in a series that starts in 2019) and stopped being fair by September. Prices rose about 1.1% from June to September, a 4.6% annualized pace, so the recent three months were not below target. The twelve-month CPI rate has been at least 2.3% every month since March 2021; the Fed's 2% target is defined on a different index (PCE), which usually runs somewhat lower, so 'above target' is shown on CPI. And a falling inflation rate does not mean falling prices: from January 2023 to September 2024 the rate fell from 6.4% to 2.4% while the price level kept rising.
whyWatch: People are told there is no inflation, that it is low by historical standards, and that it is far below the peak. The official CPI shows which of these comparisons hold and which pick a convenient baseline.
tension: Inflation is less than half its 2022 peak, which lets one side call it low. It is also higher than when the administration took office and has been above target for five years, which lets the other side call it high.

arc.hook: Depending on who you listen to, there is no inflation, or it is the worst in years. Both cannot be right.
arc.conflict: Each side picks a baseline: the 2022 peak makes today look low; January 2025 and the Fed target make it look high.
arc.evidence: The September 2026 CPI, then the same number against history, the peak, January 2025, the recent three months and the target, then the rate against the price level.
arc.resolution: Inflation is 3.7%: far below the 2022 peak, but above target, above the start of 2025 and above any year from 2024 to 2025, and not zero by any measure.
arc.takeaway: When you hear an inflation comparison, ask what it is being compared with, and remember that a lower rate still means higher prices.

questions.question: How high is US inflation right now, compared with the target, the past and the 2022 peak?

central.text: The evidence does not support "The US has no inflation [October 2026]"

questions.premise: Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September 2026 and 3.7% over twelve months, so the claim that there is no inflation is wrong. 3.7% is below the 9.1% peak of June 2022 but above every reading in 2024 and 2025, above the roughly 1.5-2.5% pace before the pandemic, and above the 3.0% of January 2025. It was a different story in January 2026: 2.4%, tied for the lowest reading since early 2021 and about the pre-pandemic pace, so 'low by historical standards' was fair then (in a series that starts in 2019) and stopped being fair by September. Prices rose about 1.1% from June to September, a 4.6% annualized pace, so the recent three months were not below target. The twelve-month CPI rate has been at least 2.3% every month since March 2021; the Fed's 2% target is defined on a different index (PCE), which usually runs somewhat lower, so 'above target' is shown on CPI. And a falling inflation rate does not mean falling prices: from January 2023 to September 2024 the rate fell from 6.4% to 2.4% while the price level kept rising.
questions.tension: Inflation is less than half its 2022 peak, which lets one side call it low. It is also higher than when the administration took office and has been above target for five years, which lets the other side call it high.
questions.whyWatch: People are told there is no inflation, that it is low by historical standards, and that it is far below the peak. The official CPI shows which of these comparisons hold and which pick a convenient baseline.

arc.hook: Depending on who you listen to, there is no inflation, or it is the worst in years. Both cannot be right.
arc.conflict: Each side picks a baseline: the 2022 peak makes today look low; January 2025 and the Fed target make it look high.
arc.evidence: The September 2026 CPI, then the same number against history, the peak, January 2025, the recent three months and the target, then the rate against the price level.
arc.resolution: Inflation is 3.7%: far below the 2022 peak, but above target, above the start of 2025 and above any year from 2024 to 2025, and not zero by any measure.
arc.takeaway: When you hear an inflation comparison, ask what it is being compared with, and remember that a lower rate still means higher prices.

questions.question: What is pushing US inflation up in 2026: gasoline, tariffs, or prices across the board?

central.text: Gasoline prices are the main driver of the recent rise in headline inflation [September 2026]

questions.premise: Headline inflation fell to 2.4% in January and February 2026, then jumped to 3.3%, 3.8% and 4.2% from March to May as gasoline rose 24.9% in March alone; the CPI tables show the energy jump but do not name its cause. In September, gasoline rose 9.1% and accounted for over half of the monthly increase. Outside energy, many major indexes rose in September (used cars, airline fares, medical care, apparel), but core inflation was 2.6% over the year, so increases have spread without core accelerating sharply. Core ran 2.4-2.9% through 2026, a little under three percent; it dipped to 2.4% in August and edged back to 2.6% in September, so 'around three and not decelerating' overstates it. Shelter rose 3.2%, faster than core. The New York Fed estimates tariffs added about 2.9 points to twelve-month inflation in the sampled consumer goods by February 2026; that is a relative effect on goods, not a measure of core CPI, so tariffs measurably raised goods prices but their share of core inflation is not pinned down.
questions.tension: If gasoline explains the rise, it should fade when fuel prices fall. If prices have broadened, or tariffs are feeding core inflation, it will not.
questions.whyWatch: Every side has a culprit: the war and gas prices, tariffs, or prices rising everywhere. The CPI breakdown shows how much each one explains.

arc.hook: Inflation was 2.4% in February. By May it was 4.2%. What changed?
arc.conflict: One side blames gasoline and the war, another blames tariffs, and a third says prices are rising everywhere.
arc.evidence: The headline path through 2026, the gasoline share of the September rise, core and shelter, then the tariff estimate and its limits.
arc.resolution: Gasoline drove most of the jump in headline inflation. Core inflation sits a little under three percent with shelter above it, and tariffs pushed up goods prices by an amount researchers can measure only relative to less-exposed goods.
arc.takeaway: Watch core inflation, not the headline: it tells you whether the rise will outlast fuel prices.
